subject: physics
title: Projectile motion
key_idea: A projectile moves with constant velocity horizontally and constant acceleration g vertically. The two motions are independent, so each is solved separately using the equations of uniform acceleration, and linked only by the time of flight.

blocks.text: A projectile moves freely under gravity alone. This section covers how its motion splits into two independent parts.

diagram.alt: A comparison of the horizontal and the vertical motion of a projectile.
items: Horizontal
Vertical

values: v = u + gt, s = ut + ½gt²

items: The horizontal component of velocity stays the same throughout the flight.
The vertical component changes steadily because of gravity.
A ball dropped and a ball fired horizontally from the same height hit the ground at the same time. Their vertical motions are identical.
The time of flight is the only quantity shared by the two motions.
Horizontal: no acceleration, constant velocity.
Vertical: constant acceleration g downwards.
Time links the two motions.

blocks.text: Resolve the initial velocity into components. Then apply the equations of uniform acceleration to each direction.

items.text: Split the launch velocity v at angle θ above the horizontal into vₓ = v cos θ and v_y = v sin θ.
Use s = ut + ½at² or v = u + at with u = v_y and a = −g (upwards positive).
Find the time of flight from the vertical motion. For a launch and landing at the same height, the vertical displacement is zero.
Use range = vₓ × t with that time.

items: For a horizontal launch, the initial vertical velocity is zero. The time to fall a height h comes from h = ½gt².
At the highest point of a projectile launched upwards, the vertical velocity is zero. The horizontal velocity is not.
Speed at any time is found by combining the two components: v = √(vₓ² + v_y²).
Its direction is given by tan θ = v_y / vₓ.
The path of the projectile is a parabola.

diagram.alt: A slider for an object launched horizontally. Changing the launch speed and the height changes the time of fall and how far it lands from the base.

items.text: A ball is kicked horizontally at 12 m/s from a cliff 45 m high. Find the distance from the base where it lands.

items: Resolve the launch velocity first. Use the vertical motion to find the time.
Horizontal distance = horizontal velocity × time of flight.

checks.q: A stone is thrown horizontally at 8.0 m/s from a bridge 20 m above water. Calculate the time to reach the water. (g = 9.81 m/s²)
For the stone in the previous question, calculate the horizontal distance travelled before it hits the water.
Explain why a projectile has constant horizontal velocity but changing vertical velocity.
checks.a: The only force is weight, which acts vertically downwards. There is no horizontal force (ignoring air resistance), so no horizontal acceleration. Gravity gives a constant vertical acceleration g, so the vertical velocity changes.

blocks.text: This course also asks for a qualitative understanding of resistive forces and their effect on motion.

items: **Friction** opposes relative motion between surfaces in contact. The difference between static and dynamic friction is not tested.
**Drag** is the resistive force on an object moving through a fluid such as air. **Lift** is a force at right angles to the motion of an object moving through a fluid.
Air resistance increases with speed.
A falling object reaches **terminal speed** when the drag force equals the driving force. The resultant force is then zero.
Air resistance shortens the range and height of a projectile. The path is no longer symmetrical, and falls more steeply than it rises.
The maximum speed of a vehicle is reached when the drag equals the driving force from the engine. A streamlined shape and a smaller frontal area increase it.
